questions.stem: How does blood leaving the lungs differ from blood arriving at the lungs?
options: It has more oxygen and less carbon dioxide
It has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
It has more glucose and less urea
It has less glucose and more urea
questions.explanation: In the alveoli oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out, so the pulmonary veins carry the most oxygenated blood in the body. The lungs do not change glucose or urea levels in any significant way.

questions.stem: Soon after a meal, which blood vessel carries blood with the highest concentration of glucose and amino acids?
options: The pulmonary vein, from the lungs to the heart
The hepatic portal vein, from the small intestine to the liver
The hepatic vein, from the liver to the inferior vena cava
The renal vein, from the kidney to the vena cava
questions.explanation: Digested nutrients are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine and carried straight to the liver in the hepatic portal vein. The liver then stores or processes some of them before blood leaves in the hepatic vein.

questions.stem: Why is the concentration of urea higher in the hepatic vein than in the hepatic portal vein?
options: The liver absorbs water from the blood, which concentrates the urea already there
The muscles release urea during exercise, which is carried in the hepatic vein
The liver breaks down excess amino acids, producing urea that enters the blood
The small intestine absorbs urea from digested food, which is carried to the liver
questions.explanation: Excess amino acids cannot be stored, so liver cells remove their amino groups (deamination) and convert the ammonia to urea, which is carried in the blood to the kidneys. Urea is not absorbed from food.

questions.stem: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, the glucose concentration in the hepatic vein is lower than in the hepatic portal vein. What explains this?
options: The liver converts excess glucose to glycogen and stores it
The liver converts excess glucose to urea and releases it
The liver uses all of the glucose as fuel for its own cells
The liver passes the excess glucose straight into the bile
questions.explanation: Under the influence of insulin, liver cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen, smoothing out the rise in blood glucose after a meal. Urea is made from amino acids, not glucose.

questions.stem: In which blood vessel is the concentration of urea lowest?
options: The renal artery
The aorta
The renal vein
The hepatic vein
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter urea out of the blood into the urine, so blood leaving them in the renal vein has the lowest urea concentration. The hepatic vein has the highest, because the liver produces urea.

questions.stem: Compared with blood entering a leg muscle during intense exercise, how does blood leaving the muscle differ?
options: More oxygen and glucose, less carbon dioxide and lactate
Less oxygen and carbon dioxide, more glucose and urea
More oxygen and lactate, less glucose and carbon dioxide
Less oxygen and glucose, more carbon dioxide and lactate
questions.explanation: Working muscle cells use oxygen and glucose in respiration and release carbon dioxide; when oxygen is short they also produce lactate by anaerobic respiration. These all pass between the cells and the blood by diffusion.

questions.stem: What does the large intestine mainly add to the blood?
options: Water and mineral salts absorbed from the remaining food material
Glucose and amino acids absorbed from digested food
Urea and carbon dioxide produced by bacteria in the gut
Oxygen absorbed from the air swallowed during eating and drinking
questions.explanation: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine. The large intestine reabsorbs much of the remaining water and salts, along with some vitamins made by gut bacteria, before faeces are eliminated.

questions.stem: Blood samples from three vessels are tested. Vessel P has the highest oxygen concentration, vessel Q has the highest urea concentration, and vessel R has the lowest urea concentration. Which vessels are they most likely to be?
options: P: aorta; Q: hepatic portal vein; R: renal artery
P: vena cava; Q: renal artery; R: hepatic vein
P: pulmonary vein; Q: hepatic vein; R: renal vein
P: pulmonary artery; Q: renal vein; R: hepatic vein
questions.explanation: The pulmonary vein carries blood just oxygenated in the lungs, the hepatic vein carries urea newly made by the liver, and the renal vein carries blood just cleared of urea by the kidneys. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.

questions.stem: Glucose concentration is almost the same in the renal artery and the renal vein, yet glucose is filtered out of the blood in the kidney. What explains this?
options: Glucose is converted to urea in the nephron and leaves in the urine instead
The kidney releases new glucose that it makes from carbon dioxide and water
Filtered glucose is reabsorbed back into the blood from the nephron tubules
Glucose molecules are too large to be filtered at the glomerulus at all
questions.explanation: Glucose is small enough to pass into the filtrate, but in a healthy person it is all reabsorbed in the tubules by active transport, so little is lost. Glucose in the urine is a sign the reabsorption capacity has been exceeded, as in untreated diabetes.

questions.stem: In what form is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
options: As hydrogencarbonate ions dissolved in the plasma
As carbon dioxide gas bubbles carried in the plasma
As glucose made from carbon dioxide in red blood cells
As urea formed from carbon dioxide in white blood cells
questions.explanation: Most carbon dioxide reacts with water, mainly inside red blood cells, and is carried as hydrogencarbonate ions in the plasma; smaller amounts are dissolved or bound to haemoglobin. Gas bubbles in blood would be dangerous.

questions.stem: How is the wall of a capillary suited to its function?
options: It is waterproof, so nothing leaks out into the tissues
It is one cell thick, giving a short distance for diffusion
It is thick and muscular, so it can withstand high pressure
It is lined with valves, so blood can flow only one way
questions.explanation: Capillary walls are a single layer of flattened endothelial cells, so oxygen, nutrients and wastes diffuse quickly between blood and tissue fluid. Thick muscular walls belong to arteries, and valves are found in veins.

questions.stem: What is the function of valves in veins?
options: To stop blood flowing backwards as it returns to the heart at low pressure
To increase the blood pressure in veins so blood can reach the capillaries
To filter bacteria out of the blood before it returns to the heart
To allow oxygen to diffuse out of the blood into the surrounding tissue
questions.explanation: Blood in veins is under low pressure, so valves prevent backflow, especially in the legs where blood must travel upwards. Exchange with tissues happens in capillaries, not through vein walls.

questions.stem: Why do arteries have thick walls with elastic fibres and smooth muscle?
options: To contain valves that stop the blood flowing backwards between each heartbeat
To withstand the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart and smooth out its surges
To allow oxygen and nutrients to diffuse quickly into the tissues they pass through
To hold large volumes of blood at low pressure as it returns slowly to the heart
questions.explanation: Each contraction of the ventricles sends blood into the arteries at high pressure; elastic walls stretch and recoil to withstand this and keep blood flowing between beats. Diffusion to tissues happens across thin capillary walls.

questions.stem: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood. Why is it still classified as an artery?
options: It connects directly to capillaries in the liver, which defines an artery
It carries blood away from the heart, which defines an artery
It carries blood at low pressure, which defines an artery
It has valves along its whole length, which defines an artery
questions.explanation: Arteries are defined by the direction of flow, away from the heart, not by oxygen content. The pulmonary artery takes deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

questions.stem: In a cross-section of tissue, a vessel has a thick wall of muscle and elastic tissue and a narrow, round lumen. Next to it is a vessel with a thin wall and a wide, irregular lumen. What are they?
options: A vein and a capillary
An artery and a vein
A vein and an artery
A capillary and an artery
questions.explanation: Arteries have thick muscular walls and a relatively narrow lumen that keeps its shape. Veins have thinner walls and a wider lumen that often looks flattened. Capillaries are far too small to have muscle layers.

questions.stem: Why does blood flow most slowly through capillary beds?
options: The total cross-sectional area of the many capillaries is very large, giving time for exchange
Each capillary has a thick muscular wall that squeezes the blood to slow it right down
Capillaries contain valves that open only once every few heartbeats to let blood through
The heart pumps blood more weakly into capillaries than it does into arteries and veins
questions.explanation: Although each capillary is narrow, there are so many that their combined cross-section is far greater than the aorta's, so blood moves slowly. This gives time for diffusion between blood and cells.

questions.stem: How does blood in the veins of the legs return to the heart against gravity?
options: The blood pressure in leg veins is higher than in the aorta, which pushes blood up
Capillaries in the legs pump blood into the veins using energy from active transport
Contracting skeletal muscles squeeze the veins, and valves keep the flow towards the heart
The veins have thick muscular walls that contract in waves to pump the blood upwards
questions.explanation: Leg muscles compress the veins when they contract, and one-way valves ensure the blood can only move towards the heart. Pressure in veins is low, so this muscle pump is important.

questions.stem: What is the main function of plasma?
options: Plugging damaged blood vessels by sticking together at the site of a wound
Transporting dissolved nutrients, hormones, wastes, proteins and heat around the body
Carrying oxygen bound to haemoglobin from the lungs to the body's tissues
Engulfing and destroying bacteria and other pathogens that enter the bloodstream
questions.explanation: Plasma is the liquid part of blood, mostly water, in which glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones, ions, plasma proteins and carbon dioxide (as hydrogencarbonate) are carried. Oxygen is carried mainly by red blood cells.

questions.stem: What is the role of platelets in the blood?
options: They help blood to clot at the site of a damaged blood vessel
They carry oxygen from the lungs to the cells of the body
They produce antibodies that attach to pathogens in the blood
They carry carbon dioxide from the cells back to the lungs
questions.explanation: Platelets are fragments of large cells from the bone marrow. At a wound they stick together and release substances that trigger clotting, which converts fibrinogen to a mesh of fibrin.

questions.stem: Mature mammalian red blood cells have no nucleus. How does this relate to their function?
options: It allows the cell to divide quickly, replacing red blood cells as they are lost
It lets the cell produce antibodies faster when a pathogen is detected
It makes the cell heavier, so it sinks into the capillaries more easily
It leaves more space for haemoglobin, so each cell can carry more oxygen
questions.explanation: Without a nucleus, the cell is packed with haemoglobin and can adopt its biconcave shape. The drawback is that red blood cells cannot divide or repair themselves, so they last only about 120 days.

questions.stem: How do white blood cells differ from red blood cells in structure and function?
options: They have no nucleus and carry oxygen, some by binding it to haemoglobin and some by dissolving it
They are fragments of cells and help clotting, some by sticking together and some by making fibrin
They are much more numerous and carry nutrients, some by absorbing glucose and some by storing fat
They have a nucleus and defend against pathogens, some by phagocytosis and some by making antibodies
questions.explanation: White blood cells are nucleated and fewer in number than red cells. Phagocytes engulf pathogens and lymphocytes produce antibodies or attack infected cells. Carrying oxygen is the job of red blood cells.

questions.stem: What happens to haemoglobin in the capillaries around the alveoli and then in the capillaries of a respiring muscle?
options: It binds glucose in the lungs and releases glucose to the muscle for respiration
It binds carbon dioxide in the lungs and releases carbon dioxide in the muscle
It binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin in the lungs and releases oxygen in the muscle
It releases oxygen in the lungs and binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin in the muscle
questions.explanation: Where oxygen concentration is high, as in the lungs, haemoglobin loads oxygen. Where oxygen concentration is low, as in respiring muscle, oxyhaemoglobin unloads it. Carbon dioxide moves the opposite way, from muscle to lungs.

questions.stem: A blood test shows a very low platelet count. Which symptom is the person most likely to have?
options: Swelling of the legs and ankles because too much water stays in the blood
Bruising easily and bleeding for longer than usual from small cuts
Feeling tired and breathless because too little oxygen is carried
Catching infections often because pathogens are not destroyed
questions.explanation: With few platelets, clots form slowly, so small injuries bleed for longer and bruises form easily. Tiredness and breathlessness suggest too few red blood cells, and frequent infections suggest a white cell problem.

questions.stem: A blood sample is spun in a centrifuge. Which description of the result is correct?
options: A straw-coloured layer of plasma on top, red blood cells at the bottom, and a thin pale layer of white cells and platelets between
A red layer of plasma on top, white blood cells at the bottom, and a thin layer of red blood cells and platelets between
A white layer of platelets on top, plasma at the bottom, and a thick layer of red and white blood cells between
An even red mixture throughout, because the cells and plasma in blood cannot be separated from each other
questions.explanation: The denser cells sink: red cells at the bottom, with a thin 'buffy coat' of white cells and platelets above them. Plasma, slightly more than half the volume, forms the pale yellow top layer.

questions.stem: Which plasma protein is converted into fibrin during blood clotting?
options: Haemoglobin
Insulin
Albumin
Fibrinogen
questions.explanation: Fibrinogen is a soluble plasma protein that is converted to insoluble fibrin threads, which trap blood cells to form a clot. Haemoglobin is inside red blood cells and carries oxygen.

questions.stem: Which feature of the alveoli makes gas exchange efficient?
options: A dry inner surface that stops gases dissolving before they diffuse
A small total surface area that keeps gases close together
Very thin walls, one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance
Thick muscular walls that pump air in and out of each alveolus
questions.explanation: Alveolar walls and capillary walls are each a single thin layer of cells, so gases diffuse only a tiny distance. The surface is moist, and the total surface area is very large.

questions.stem: How do breathing and blood flow keep gas exchange in the alveoli efficient?
options: They push oxygen across the alveolar walls by active transport using energy from the breathing muscles
They keep the alveoli dry so that oxygen does not dissolve in the moisture lining the alveoli
They slow the movement of blood so that it stays in the lung capillaries until it is completely full
They maintain steep concentration gradients by bringing fresh air in and carrying oxygenated blood away
questions.explanation: Ventilation keeps oxygen high and carbon dioxide low in the alveoli, while blood flow removes oxygenated blood and brings deoxygenated blood. This keeps the gradients steep, so diffusion stays fast. Gas exchange is passive.

questions.stem: Emphysema breaks down the walls between alveoli, forming fewer, larger air spaces. Why does this make a person breathless?
options: The number of red blood cells falls, so less oxygen can be carried in the blood
The airways become wider, so too much air enters the lungs with each breath
The surface area for gas exchange is reduced, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood
The alveoli become thinner, so oxygen diffuses into the blood far too quickly
questions.explanation: Fewer, larger air spaces have much less total surface area than many small alveoli, so less oxygen can enter the blood per breath. The disease damages lung tissue; it does not directly change red cell numbers.

questions.stem: Why is the inner surface of the alveoli always moist?
options: Oxygen must dissolve in the moisture before it can diffuse across the walls
Water lubricates the alveoli so they can slide past each other when breathing
Moisture traps all bacteria so that no pathogens reach the blood
Water is the source of the oxygen that diffuses into the blood
questions.explanation: Gases diffuse across cell membranes in solution, so oxygen first dissolves in the thin film of fluid lining the alveoli. The oxygen comes from inhaled air, not from the water.

questions.stem: A student models the lungs with a bunch of small balloons attached to branching straws. Which is the most important limitation of this model?
options: It does not show that the many small sacs give a larger surface than one large balloon
It does not show that air reaches the sacs through a branching system of tubes
It does not show the thin, moist walls or the capillary network around each alveolus
It does not show that the air spaces end in many small sacs at the end of branching tubes
questions.explanation: The model does represent branching airways and many small sacs with a large surface area. It cannot show the features that make diffusion fast: walls one cell thick, a moist lining and the dense capillary network.

questions.stem: Which is the correct path of an oxygen molecule from the air to haemoglobin?
options: Alveolar air → alveolar wall → capillary wall → plasma → red blood cell
Alveolar air → capillary wall → red blood cell → alveolar wall → plasma
Alveolar air → plasma → alveolar wall → red blood cell → capillary wall
Alveolar air → red blood cell → plasma → capillary wall → alveolar wall
questions.explanation: Oxygen dissolves in the alveolar lining, diffuses through the alveolar wall and then the capillary wall into the plasma, and finally into a red blood cell, where it binds haemoglobin.

questions.stem: What are the two main functions of the kidneys?
options: Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide, and producing new red blood cells
Removing nitrogenous wastes such as urea, and regulating water and salt levels
Producing urea from amino acids, and storing excess glucose in the form of glycogen
Absorbing nutrients from digested food, and producing digestive enzymes
questions.explanation: The kidneys excrete urea and adjust the water and salt content of the blood. Urea is made in the liver, and glycogen is stored in the liver and muscles.

questions.stem: What happens during glomerular filtration in a nephron?
options: Glucose and amino acids are actively pumped from the filtrate back into the blood
Hydrogen ions and some drugs are secreted from the blood into the collecting duct
Red blood cells and plasma proteins are pushed into the filtrate and then excreted in urine
Blood pressure forces water and small solutes from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule
questions.explanation: High pressure in the glomerulus forces water, glucose, salts, urea and other small molecules into the capsule, while cells and large proteins stay in the blood. Pumping glucose back is selective reabsorption, a later step.

questions.stem: On what process does haemodialysis mainly depend to remove urea from a patient's blood?
options: Conversion of urea to glucose by enzymes in the dialysis membrane
Diffusion of urea across a partially permeable membrane into dialysis fluid
Active transport of urea by carrier proteins in the dialysis machine's tubing
Phagocytosis of urea by white blood cells added to the dialysis fluid
questions.explanation: Blood flows past a partially permeable membrane with dialysis fluid on the other side; urea diffuses down its concentration gradient into the fluid. The machine has no living cells to carry out active transport.

questions.stem: Why does dialysis fluid contain glucose at the same concentration as normal blood?
options: So glucose reacts with urea in the fluid and turns it into water
So the fluid is sweet enough to stop bacteria growing inside the machine's tubing
So there is no concentration gradient, and the patient's glucose is not lost
So glucose diffuses into the blood and gives the patient extra energy
questions.explanation: With equal concentrations on both sides, there is no net diffusion of glucose, so useful glucose stays in the blood. The same principle is used for salts: their concentration is set so only the excess diffuses out.

questions.stem: Why does fresh dialysis fluid contain no urea?
options: Because urea molecules are too large to cross the membrane in either direction
Because urea would be pumped back into the blood by the dialysis membrane
To keep the urea concentration gradient from blood to fluid as steep as possible
To stop urea from reacting with the glucose that is dissolved in the fluid
questions.explanation: Urea moves by diffusion from where it is concentrated (the blood) to where it is not (the fluid). Fluid with no urea gives the steepest gradient, so as much urea as possible is removed.

questions.stem: In a dialyser, blood and dialysis fluid flow in opposite directions on either side of the membrane. Why?
options: Countercurrent flow lets urea and glucose cross in opposite directions so they swap places
Countercurrent flow stops the blood and fluid from mixing, which would happen if they ran parallel
Countercurrent flow keeps a concentration gradient along the whole membrane, removing more urea
Countercurrent flow increases the pressure in the blood, so cells are filtered out more quickly
questions.explanation: Flowing in opposite directions means the blood always meets fluid with a lower urea concentration than itself, so diffusion continues along the whole length. With parallel flow the concentrations would even out partway along.

questions.stem: Which comparison of renal dialysis with a healthy kidney is correct?
options: Dialysis removes wastes by diffusion a few times a week; kidneys filter continuously and selectively reabsorb useful substances
Dialysis selectively reabsorbs glucose by active transport; kidneys remove all substances by diffusion alone
Dialysis works all day and night without stopping; kidneys work only for a few hours several times a week
Dialysis also produces hormones such as EPO; kidneys remove only urea and have no other functions
questions.explanation: Haemodialysis is typically done in sessions of several hours, often about three times a week, so wastes and fluid build up between sessions. Kidneys work continuously, use active transport for reabsorption and secretion, and also produce hormones.

questions.stem: Before a patient's blood enters the dialysis machine, a substance such as heparin is added. Why?
options: To prevent the blood from clotting as it passes through the tubing
To give the blood the glucose it loses by diffusion into the fluid
To kill any bacteria that are present in the patient's blood
To make urea molecules small enough to pass through the membrane
questions.explanation: Contact with artificial surfaces can trigger clotting, which would block the dialyser, so an anticoagulant such as heparin is added. Glucose is not lost, because the fluid contains glucose at blood concentration.

questions.stem: Many people with kidney failure on long-term dialysis develop anaemia and are given injections of erythropoietin (EPO). Why?
options: The dialysis membrane filters out red blood cells, so EPO is needed to stop them leaving the blood
EPO helps urea diffuse across the dialysis membrane, so less time is needed on the machine
EPO converts urea into amino acids, so the patient's blood contains less urea between sessions
Healthy kidneys make EPO, which stimulates red blood cell production, and dialysis cannot replace this
questions.explanation: The kidney is also an endocrine organ: when blood oxygen is low, it releases EPO, which stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells. Dialysis only removes wastes and excess fluid, so it cannot replace this hormone function.
